title: Strings, UTF-8, and slices

spans.text: LESSON PURPOSE

Goal: apply “Strings, UTF-8, and slices” to a real program or device. The key principle is: `String` owns the text; `&str` borrows a view. In a project, follow this guidance: Use `String` when text must be owned or changed; accept `&str` when a function only needs to read it.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.
EXAMPLE CODE
EXPECTED RESULT
Rust
CORE EXPLANATION

A Rust `String` owns growable UTF-8 text on the heap; `&str` is a borrowed view. UTF-8 characters can use multiple bytes, so `text[0]` indexing is unavailable: `len()` counts bytes, while `chars()` iterates Unicode scalar values. A slice views part of text or an array without copying it; a function accepting `&str` can work with both a `String` and a string literal.
IMPORTANT LINE BREAKDOWN

Key line: `text.split_whitespace().next().unwrap_or("")`
What it does: `String` owns the text; `&str` borrows a view.
Why it is used: Use `String` when text must be owned or changed; accept `&str` when a function only needs to read it.
If omitted or changed: UTF-8 byte boundaries are not character boundaries; `&text[..1]` is not a safe character slice for every string.

SECOND PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

spans.code:
fn last_word(text: &str) -> &str { text.split_whitespace().last().unwrap_or("") }
fn main() { println!("{}", last_word("safe borrowed view")); }
